questions.question: In Creationeering™, what is the main idea behind the "Death & Recycling" phase for a product?

options.A: To quickly get rid of old products to make room for new ones.
options.B: To responsibly manage materials and resources even after a product is no longer useful.
options.C: To only focus on the initial design and cost of a product.
options.D: To make sure products last forever without ever needing to be recycled.

questions.explanation: The Death & Recycling phase emphasizes our ethical responsibility to God's creation by stewarding resources even after a product's useful life.

questions.question: The lesson connects the Creationeering™ phase of Death & Recycling to a biblical truth found in Ecclesiastes 1:4-7. What is this biblical truth that inspires our approach to product end-of-life?

options.A: That humans are meant to conquer and control all of nature.
options.B: That God's creation is full of continuous cycles and renewal.
options.C: That all things eventually come to a complete and final end.
options.D: That only new creations are valuable in God's eyes.

questions.explanation: Ecclesiastes 1:4-7 highlights the endless cycles of nature, reminding us that God's creation is a masterwork of renewal, which inspires our approach to Death & Recycling.

questions.question: An engineer is designing a new type of biodegradable plastic for packaging. They want the plastic to break down quickly after use (Objective), but it must also be strong enough to protect the product inside (Constraint). The engineer can choose different chemical formulas for the plastic (Variable). Which part of this scenario represents the "Constraint" in the OCV method?

options.A: Designing a new type of biodegradable plastic.
options.B: The plastic needing to be strong enough to protect the product.
options.C: The plastic breaking down quickly after use.
options.D: Choosing different chemical formulas for the plastic.

questions.explanation: A constraint is a limitation or restriction that must be satisfied in a design problem, such as the plastic needing to be strong enough.

questions.question: When a skateboard wheel wears down over time (a large-scale observation), the lesson explains that this is because tiny bonds between rubber molecules are breaking due to friction (a small-scale cause). What is this way of connecting observations at different sizes called?
questions.explanation: Multiscale Modeling is the process of connecting observations at large scales (like a worn wheel) to their underlying causes at smaller, often atomic, scales (like breaking molecular bonds).

questions.question: The lesson describes "reprocessing" as giving materials a fresh start by transforming them into something entirely different. How is reprocessing different from simply "recycling" a material?

options.A: Recycling uses new materials, while reprocessing uses old materials.
options.B: Reprocessing turns materials into something new and different, while recycling often makes the same type of product again.
options.C: Recycling is more expensive than reprocessing.
options.D: Reprocessing only applies to natural materials, while recycling applies to man-made materials.

questions.explanation: Reprocessing involves transforming materials into something entirely different, whereas recycling often means converting a material into a new product of the same type (e.g., an old can into a new can).
